q-37515.name: Question 1
q-37515.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(0,-1,1).$
q-37515.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)k \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2y)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,-1,1) & =(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\text{ }i+[(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+2(-1)]\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =-i-2\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x=\frac{y+1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}
$$

q-37570.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$
q-37570.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(y+5)\text{ }i+x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(-1+5)\,i+(1)\,j+2(2)\,k \\  & =4\,i+j+4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $4\,i+j+4\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$

Question 2
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+z2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2).

a
i+2j+4k
b
4i−2j+4k
c
4j+k
d
−4i−2k
e
4i+j+4k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2) can be found by computing ∇f(1,−1,2).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(xy+5x+z2)i+∂∂y(xy+5x+z2)j+∂∂z(xy+5x+z2)k=(y+5) i+x j+2z k∇f(1,−1,2)=(−1+5)i+(1)j+2(2)k=4i+j+4k

Therefore, 4i+j+4k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2).

q-71400.name: Question 3
q-71400.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1).$
q-71400.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,1,1) & =\frac{1}{1}\,i+\frac{1}{1}\,j+\frac{1}{1}\,k \\  & =i+j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i+j+k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1).$

q-71407.name: Question 4
q-71407.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$
q-71407.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

?

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface z=2x2+2y2+x at the point (12,1,3).

a
r=⟨3,−4,1⟩+t⟨12,1,3⟩
b
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨3,4,1⟩
c
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨3,−4,1⟩
d
r=⟨−3,−4,1⟩+t⟨12,1,3⟩
e
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨−3,−4,1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side:

z=2x2+2y2+xz−2x2−2y2−x=0

If we set f(x,y,z)=z−2x2−2y2−x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (12,1,3) can be found by computing ∇f(12,1,3).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (12,1,3):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(z−2x2−2y2−x)i+∂∂y(z−2x2−2y2−x)j+∂∂z(z−2x2−2y2−x)k=(−4x−1) i−4y j+k∇f(12,1,3)=(−4(12)−1)i−4(1) j+k=−3i−4j+k=⟨−3,−4,1⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(12,1,3) and passes through the point (12,1,3) can be written as

r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t∇f(12,1,3)=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨−3,−4,1⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).

q-130720.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{3}{y}^{2}=2x+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,1).$
q-130720.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}{y}^{2} & =2x+y \\ {x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2)\,i+(2{x}^{3}y-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =(3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}-2)\,i+(2(-1)^{3}(1)-1)\,j \\  & =\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,1)=⟨1,-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x+1) & =y-1 \\ -3x-3 & =y-1 \\ 3x+y+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$
